Proficiency-based graduation requirements: building principal must certify all proficiency requirements; students pursue proficiency in six content areas per year including English Language Arts and Literacy
Proficiency areas: English Language Arts & Literacy, Mathematics, Science, Global Citizenship, Physical Education, Health, Fine Arts
Personalized learning plan (PLP) developed and updated by each student
Credit is earned in a high school course only with an overall course grade of at least 1.5 (not applied to Transferable Skills or Habits of Work)
College courses and AP courses are weighted at 1.1 course credits
Class standing for 2026-27: Sophomore 7 credits, Junior 14, Senior 21
Course load: four classes each semester; full-time students in grades 9-11 carry eight credits during the school year
graduation_requirements.raw_text:
Quarry Valley Graduation Requirements
Current
English - 4.0 credits
Global Citizenship - 4.0 credits
Mathematics - 4.0 credits
Science - 4.0 credits
Physical Education - 2.0 credits
Health - 1.0 credits
Fine Art/Music - 1.0 credit
World Language/World Culture - 1.0 credits
Electives - 7.0 credits
Total: 28 credits
In order to be awarded a diploma and to participate in the graduation ceremony the building
principal must certify that the student has successfully completed all of the proficiency
requirements for graduation. Students must be pursuing proficiency in six content areas per year
including English Language Arts and Literacy. Please contact the guidance office if you wish to
review your child’s four-year plan or if you have further questions. Students will be working on
developing and updating their own personalized learning plans (PLP). Their personalized
learning plan will outline the student’s pathway in pursuit of proficiency in the content area
required for graduation whether through coursework or internship experience(s).

courses.description: Students will be introduced to high school level proficiencies through direct instruction of texts, literary terms, and structures (both nonfiction and fiction). This course also stresses the continued improvement of writing skills with special emphasis on organization and development. This course focuses on the review of the fundamentals of grammar and usage as well as introducing a variety of literary genres such as: the short story, poetry, drama and the novel. The course is designed to teach the process skills of reading comprehension and the writing process.

Students will read diverse literature from around the world in a variety of mediums including novels, poetry, drama, short stories, non-fiction, and graphic novels. This course will focus on developing both written and oral communication skills to prepare students to engage in fluent and responsible communication and to analyze information that comes to them in many forms of expression.

American Literature will focus on critical analysis, which focuses on the standards and grade level expectations, with writing assignments designed for the students to continue their development as discriminating learners. There will be an emphasis placed on research of both primary and secondary documents. This course will include novels, plays, poems, and short stories. Writing will reflect the themes present in these works, and class discussion will revolve around thinking deeply about who we are as Americans and as individuals.

The AP English Literature and Composition course focuses on reading, analyzing, and writing about imaginative literature (fiction, poetry, drama) from various periods. Students engage in close reading and critical analysis of imaginative literature to deepen their understanding of the ways writers use language to provide both meaning and pleasure. As they read, students consider a work’s structure, style, and themes, as well as its use of figurative language, imagery, and symbolism. Writing assignments include expository, analytical, and argumentative essays that require students to analyze and interpret literary works. Please note that this is designed to be a fast-paced and highly demanding course. This course prepares students to take the College Board’s exam in May.

The AP English Language and Composition course focuses on the development and revision of evidence-based analytic and argumentative writing, the rhetorical analysis of nonfiction texts, and the decisions writers make as they compose and revise. Students evaluate, synthesize, and cite research to support their arguments. Additionally, they read and analyze rhetorical elements and their effects in nonfiction texts—including images as forms of text—from a range of disciplines and historical periods. Please note that this is designed to be a fast-paced and highly demanding course. This course prepares students to take the College Board’s exam in May.

Using a variety of literary texts, students will explore the deeper aspects of the human experience. Students will read and write about subjects such as love, death, failure, and redemption, with in-depth discussions on finding meaning in suffering and winning internal struggles. As students wrestle with these essential questions, they will complete vigorous activities for the purpose of enhancing English language arts skills.

Students will enhance their understanding of and appreciation for literature by drafting their own creative works. Through the workshop process, students will give and receive feedback in order to revise their drafts into a portfolio of highly polished fiction, poetry, and ten-minute plays. Throughout the course, students will refine their knowledge of literary devices, as well as writing forms and techniques, and they will be able to cite examples from the assigned readings during class discussions and presentations.

Do you like variety? This course will be a fictional "tasting supper" and will include a variety of genres: myths, fables/fantasy; short stories (mystery/detective, sci-fi/horror, action/adventure, young romance, historical fiction) and one act plays. Students will read outstanding examples from each genre, write and share their own brief works in these styles, dramatize some of these works, and present them to audiences of peers and/or elementary school students. On occasion, they will guide younger students as these students write, illustrate or act out stories from the genres.

In this course, students will develop basic competencies and functional skills in the areas of listening, speaking, reading and writing. Instruction is interactive and multi-sensory. Attention is given to developing decoding and encoding skills in reading and written language, as well as reading comprehension using literature, newspapers and other high-interest low-level reading materials. Recommendation of teacher(s) is required.

What inspires us to endure in the face of devastating and seemingly insurmountable obstacles? From survival of the human spirit to survival of the species, this course will explore fiction, non-fiction, poetry, and film to analyze and discuss the true meaning of survival. Through individual inquiry and group discussion, students will examine the writer's craft and historical context to determine the theme and purpose of each piece.

Civics will examine what it means to be an American. Students will learn about the foundations of the American political system, and what values and principles are basic to American constitutional democracy. Students will learn about the relationship we as citizens have with our government and will examine the rights and responsibilities of citizens. The course also examines the structure of the U.S. government and how it functions.

Global Studies will examine world history, world cultures, and international relations from the 1400s into modern times. Emphasis will be placed on current events as they relate to historical events. This course is designed to give students opportunities to learn about our increasingly interdependent world.

U.S. History is a survey of US history from the Civil War era to modern times. Topics may include industrialization, immigration, globalization, war and peace, civil rights and significant political, socioeconomic, and cultural developments in the U.S. since the Civil War.

Sports and Society examines the historical development and role of sport in American society and culture. Students examine the relationship between sport and the social, economic, cultural and political forces at work in the United States and in the broader world. Examination includes historical contextualization as well as the impact of gender, race, ethnicity and class.
courses.notes: Tag printed as "WRH" (presumed West Rutland High School)

courses.description: Modern U.S. History explores the key events and cultural shifts in the United States since 1945. This engaging class examines post-World War II society, the Cold War, U.S. foreign relations, the Korean and Vietnam Wars, the impactful social and political movements of the 1960s, and America's involvement in the Middle East. We will also discuss the ongoing divide between liberalism and conservatism and the evolution of contemporary American culture. Join us to uncover the compelling stories that have shaped modern America.
courses.notes: No school tag in catalog; a separate entry "Modern US History (PoHS)" also exists

courses.description: This course works with students needing an additional year of development and reiteration of essential math concepts covered in middle school essential for them to be successful in high school mathematics. Students will use hands-on and collaborative learning approaches to develop their understanding of topics including fractions, ratios and proportions, expressions and equations, linear functions, geometry, and statistics. Students will continuously build off current understandings and make connections to real world situations while developing strong problem solving skills.

Algebra 1 begins with a basic review of order of operations, ratios, and proportions leading into the topic of Observed and Theoretical Probability. Students will study the different forms of linear equations, intercept form, standard form, and point-slope form and apply the various forms to real world applications. Students will study systems of linear equations and systems of inequalities with the focus on graphing, substitution and elimination methods with an introduction to matrices. Students will study exponents and exponential equations involving exponential growth and decay. Students will study rational functions; linear, exponential, and quadratic. The focus toward the end of the course will be working with polynomials, multiplying and factoring, the zero product property, and roots of quadratic equations.

A study of Mathematics that begins with undefined and defined terms. Students use the undefined and defined terms throughout the course to build a basic understanding of mathematical systems. Students study the topics of inductive and deductive reasoning, congruence of polygons, similarity of geometric figures, properties of circles, area of regular and complex geometric figures as well as the volume of geometric solids. Students explore the geometric concepts throughout the course using classical construction tools, the compass and straightedge. Students will also use their knowledge of Algebra to study aspects of coordinate geometry, the Pythagorean Theorem, and introductory trigonometry.

In this course students’ understanding of prior algebra skills and concepts will be extended to include topics essential to a second year course. Topics include recursion, data analysis, linear systems, functions, transformations, exponents and logarithms, polynomial functions, conic sections, rational functions, and trigonometry. Graphing calculators and appropriate technology will be used to enhance understanding and extend exploration in many areas. This course is open to all students who have successfully completed proficiencies in Algebra I and Geometry.

This course emphasizes basic trigonometry concepts, equations, identities, graphs, inverse relations, complex numbers, polar coordinates and applied problems in the first semester. In the second semester topics covered include conic sections, logarithms and exponents, sequences and series, limits and some probability and statistics if time permits. In addition to creating a basic understanding of these topics, the course will also lay a foundation for Calculus or other advanced mathematics courses students may encounter in college.

This dual enrollment course is an introduction to the basic ideas and techniques of probability and statistics. Topics may include numerical and graphical descriptive measures, probability, random variables, the normal distribution, sampling theory, estimation, hypothesis testing, correlation, and regression. The use of technology may be required. Students must take a math assessment for placement purposes prior to registration. Prerequisite: Math & Algebra for College or equivalent skills. Prerequisite: Students must have completed Algebra II.

Foundations level courses will be for students who need to develop the basic and functional life skills in the content area of the course. These are students who will benefit from small groups and a hands-on approach to learning. This course is designed for those students requiring instruction on basic knowledge in math for everyday living. Units vary yearly depending on the needs of the students in the class. Examples of units include, Money: values of dollars and cents, making change, purchasing items; Order of Operations: addition and subtraction (intro multiplication and division IF the students in the class are functioning at the appropriate levels to do so); Time - hours, minutes, seconds, reading a clock; Base Ten. Recommendation of teacher(s) is required.

Understanding financial management concepts is an important life skill. From credit to insurance to taxes, it is imperative that students understand the consequences of their choices. A thorough understanding of financial concepts, with practical application through activities and projects, will enable students to leave this course with applicable useful skills for life. This course surveys the basic personal financial needs of most individuals and emphasizes the basics of budgeting, saving, checking, debt, consumer awareness, investments and credit. Students will build strong money habits early on and avoid many of the mistakes that lead to lifelong money struggles.
courses.fulfills_text: This course can be the fourth math course needed for West Rutland School’s minimum graduation requirement for math education, it could also be considered a business course, or an elective course depending on the students’ needs for completing their graduation requirements.

courses.description: Earth Science is the first high school course in science. Earth Science is the study of the world around you. In this course, students will study earth, both as it exists by itself, and as part of the solar system. Topics and themes include the structure of the earth, astronomy, the atmosphere, weather, climate, geology, and the impacts humans have on the planet. Students may choose to work towards earning Honors, with increased expectations.

Biology is the scientific study of living organisms. Students participating in this course will develop an understanding of the principles of biology including, lab safety, scientific processes, ecology, cells, genetics, evolution and the six kingdoms. The course considers the interactions among the vast number of organisms that inhabit planet Earth. It presents the basic form and function of these organisms, from cells to organ systems, and simple to complex cellular structure. It delves into interactions between organisms, and between an organism and its environment. Laboratory work, hands-on activities and some dissections will help students on their journey through the amazing living world. Students may choose to work towards earning Honors, with increased expectations.

Chemistry is the study of the composition and properties of substances, and the changes that such substances can undergo. Students will explore the fundamental principles of chemistry which characterize the properties of matter and how it reacts. Topics may include, but are not limited to: measurement, atomic structure, electron configuration, the periodic table bonding, gas laws, properties of liquids and solids, solutions, stoichiometry, reactions, kinetics, equilibrium, and acids and bases. Students may choose to work towards earning Honors, with increased expectations. To be successful at the Honors level work, students should have strong algebra and proportional reasoning skills. Prerequisite: Students must have completed Earth Science, Algebra I and Geometry or instructor permission.
courses.prerequisites: Students must have completed Earth Science, Algebra I and Geometry or instructor permission.

courses.description: Forensic Science I is designed to introduce students to key concepts and methods of forensic science, more commonly known as crime-scene investigation. To be successful in this course, students should be working toward meeting proficiency in Biology. Forensic Science is designed to introduce students to key concepts and methods of forensic science, more commonly known as crime-scene investigation. This course will include the following units of study: observation skills, evidence collection, death, fingerprints, DNA fingerprinting, blood and blood spatter, hair, fibers and textiles, pollen and spores, toxicology, handwriting analysis, soil, glass, forensic anthropology, casts and impressions, tool marks, and ballistics. This is a fast-paced hands-on course with frequent laboratory exercises embedded into class time. Prerequisite: Students must have completed or be enrolled in Biology.
courses.prerequisites: Students must have completed or be enrolled in Biology.

courses.description: Foundations level courses will be for students who need to develop the basic and functional life skills in the content area of the course. These are students who will benefit from small groups and a hands-on approach to learning. This course is designed for those students requiring instruction in basic knowledge of the elements of science for everyday living. Students will be able to have an overall understanding of plants and animals, natural resources in the world, and the human body. Units rotate depending on the needs of the students in the class. Recommendation of teacher(s) is required.

Students in physical education classes follow a structured curriculum focusing on two areas: individual/team sports and introduction to fitness. The individual/team sports curriculum includes a variety of activities designed to enhance self-confidence, group dynamics, and coordination and movement skills. The introduction to fitness curriculum focuses on the five components of fitness, instructing students in the basics of exercise physiology and providing insight into the importance of life-time activities. Students are assessed on their ability to successfully complete required activities and class projects. Teachers use a grading rubric to help students understand expectations and track performance. As in all physical education classes, each student will be evaluated on participation, attitude, projects and/or written tests.

3 standards the whole class will be based around: 1.Selects and participates in physical activities (e.g., dance, yoga, aerobics) that meet the need for self-expression. 2.Applies knowledge of movement sequences to create or participate in one or more forms of dance. 3.Demonstrates appropriate technique in flexibility training. In this class we will practice mobility routines to increase our flexibility. Self expression will be explored by researching dance genres, choreographing short dances, practicing several yoga methods, engaging in pilates and imagery. Come try these lifetime fitness activities so you can grow your knowledge and tap into the benefits of each.

Students learn about the health related fitness components, healthy lifestyles, nutrition and other aspects of health and wellness. This physical education class performs various types of workouts three days a week. Students will learn to self-monitor through reflections, self-assessing and producing a wellness portfolio. Students will develop a fitness and nutrition plan and have the semester to try to work towards and achieve these goals. The goal of this course is to allow students to investigate topics around fitness and wellness in today's society while being able to work towards current health goals.
courses.notes: No school tag in catalog (a separate "Fitness and Nutrition (PrHS)" 1 credit entry also exists)

courses.description: To build students' health knowledge and skills development in an effort to prepare and empower students to value and engage in healthy lifestyles. The course content includes: body structure, human growth and development, family and mental health, nutrition, prevention of disease, safety, personal health habits, drugs and alcohol. The skills that will be developed in this class are: decision making, communication skills, examination of values and attitudes, location and evaluation of health related information, application and coping skills.

The Art Curriculum is divided into four proficiencies; creating, presenting, responding, and connecting. Studio Art is a course designed for students to pursue their understanding of these proficiencies independently. Students research topics of personal interest and develop skills in their desired media. They use a plethora of critique methods to design, revise and create personal works of art. They develop an accurate, detailed, specific, visual arts vocabulary that allows them to engage in meaningful conversation as they respond to their artwork and the work of others. Students help to set deadlines for projects according to their personal goals.

Chorus is a performing group open to all students in grades 7 through 12. This class is for singers of all ability levels. We learn how to use our voices properly, to sing the best we can. We sing a variety of music and learn what it means to sing well as a group. Teamwork is the name of the game. The West Rutland School chorus sings a number of concerts throughout the year. This course runs for 2 semesters on M, W and F only. Students may choose to be in both band and chorus on alternating days.
courses.notes: Tag: WRS. Catalog: open to all students in grades 7 through 12; runs 2 semesters on M, W and F only

courses.description: Band is a performing group open to all students who are interested in playing an instrument. Students will study various styles of music, learn about reading music, and learn how to work together as an ensemble. There will be multiple concerts and parades throughout the year. All band members are required to attend all rehearsals and concerts, and march in all parades. This course runs for 2 semesters on M, W and F only. Students may choose to be in both band and chorus on alternating days.
courses.notes: Tag: WRS. Runs 2 semesters on M, W and F only

courses.description: This is an introductory course for students to learn music from around the world focusing on percussion, cultural awareness and music history. Proper technique on a variety of instruments (Primarily Djembe and Congas) and beginning music theory provide the framework for learning different song styles. “Hit Stuff”: World Percussion explores music from around the world, but will focus on rhythms from Africa, Brazil, Latin America, Blue Man Group, and Stomp. Music theory and notation are an integral part of the curriculum. This is not primarily geared toward performance (like Chorus, Band, and Rock Lab), but the class may be occasionally called on to play rhythms at school activities. Teaching/Learning Style: Students learn to play a variety of percussion instruments in class through group playing and listening. Studying the music’s societal influence from different cultures deepens the awareness of the music and drumming as a universal language. There is no music prerequisite, and no musical training is needed before taking the class.

Open to students who already play guitar or drums. This class will explore techniques unique to jazz and rock music. Curriculum will include chord progressions, scales, style analysis and 20th century music history through listening
courses.notes: Tag: WRS. Open to students who already play guitar or drums

courses.description: Students will learn to understand spoken Spanish using vocabulary and constructions appropriate for the earliest phases of language learning. Students work toward proficiency in listening, speaking, reading, writing, and cultural competency. Students will be able to answer questions, and ask these questions in the appropriate situations. Students will follow and carry on basic conversations using familiar construction and vocabulary. Students will read and write all material learned orally. Countries in which Spanish is spoken will be culturally explored.

Students will review and expand upon vocabulary and constructions previously studied. Class activities will be conducted increasingly in Spanish, and students are expected to actively participate, utilizing the language as much as possible. Reading and writing skills will be developed. Works in Spanish will be read. Cultural elements and current events will be explored. Prerequisite: Successful completion of Spanish I

Students will continue to review and develop vocabulary and learn more complex structures and concepts inherent to Spanish language and culture. Students will speak Spanish in class. Journal writing and individual language projects will be emphasized. Literature will continue to be explored and additional works read. Prerequisite: Successful completion of Spanish I & Spanish II. To take Spanish IV, Spanish III must be successfully completed.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Spanish I & Spanish II.

courses.description: This class is an in-depth look at the broadcast media industry, including an introduction to anchoring, directing, editing, interviewing, news writing, photojournalism, video, and reporting. This course will be technology based through its use of audio and visual equipment, video editing, and production.

Our new food and culture class helps students identify the relationship between food and its meaning while exploring the culture in which it originates from. Students travel the world, looking at how the geography of a country, as well as its political and agricultural landscape, shape the way that food is made and even eaten! Students will also look at different ethnic groups and parts of culture and how they influence choices that are made for when food is eaten as well as how it is eaten. Field trips to various locations and guest cooks help to deepen students' understanding of the content that is being taught with daily cooking classes based on the country that is being studied each week.

This course is an introduction to all the fundamental aspects of theater. Students will read a variety of plays progressing through the history of theater while concurrently learning about dramatic structure, and exploring the fundamentals of theatrical design and performance.

Student enrollment in Driver’s Education is limited to 20 students per class, and selection will be prioritized by student’s date of birth. A student must have a valid Vermont Learner’s permit on the first day of class. A proficiency grade will be issued for driver’s education. This course consists of five parts: ● Classroom component (at least 30 hours) which may be conducted in-person or remotely. ● Behind the wheel component (at least 6 hours), The B-T-W and observation time is done in the Driver education vehicle. ● Observation component (at least 6 hours) ● Parent/Guardian component (practice driving time). Parent component is 40 hours of supervised practice driving time of which 25 hours is during student enrollment in the Driver Education Course. ● Social Responsibility component (student’s attitudes and behaviors). Students are expected to follow appropriate GRCSU Health and Safety Guidelines, demonstrate self-respect to themselves and others, think before they act, accept responsibility for their actions, participate in group discussions and follow the rules in the school setting and outside on the road. If minimum attendance requirements are not met, the student will be dropped from the course. How is a student assessed? (Learning Target/Course Assessments) ● In the classroom phase, the student must score at least proficient on each unit discussed, and score at least 80 on the final exam. ● Students must show they are responsible citizens with socially responsible attitudes and behaviors. Attitudes and behaviors will have a bearing on whether students will receive a Driver Education Completion Certificate. ● In the driving phase, the student will have a driving route to practice various techniques and skills. ● Students will be given a mock final road test for their final drive. They must score at least 80% proficiency on the Driver Education Final Road Test. ● Parents will be required to attend a parent meeting or schedule an initial check-in meeting with the instructor. What will Driver Education students learn? (Enduring Understanding/Indicators) The classroom has nine units of knowledge and understanding. It includes but is not limited to the following: Getting ready to drive, understanding driver vehicle readiness, laws of the road, basic driving, maneuvers (parallel park, VT Turnaround, and hill start), managing risks, time and space, rural and city driving, interstate driving, impaired driving, distracted driving, use of the safety systems, physics and car crashes, biology and car crashes, adverse conditions, environmental issues, insurance, basic car and tire maintenance, and trip planning.

courses.course_name: Career Exploration and Post Secondary Planning
courses.description: This course is the second half of Drivers Ed. In Career Exploration, students will take a look at various post secondary opportunities, career options and how their personal interests, aptitudes, and values fit into the overall picture of choosing a fitting career. The students will have an opportunity to see different college and career paths, and talk to speakers to gain a better understanding as to how they can take their education and transition into a career opportunity. Students will also take a look at goal-setting and the decision making process in order to better understand how decisions we make today can affect our futures. During this quarter course students will: ● Explore post secondary planning, careers, and paths that will lead them to make the right choices towards their future ● Have the opportunity to talk to professionals both in and outside of the classroom ● Take field trips to enhance their understand of different post secondary opportunities, college, careers, and professions ● Complete a research project based on one career of interest Students will demonstrate their understanding of different careers during a community based presentation at the end of the quarter where they will present their findings to the elementary school.
courses.notes: Tags: WRS, PrHS, PoHS. Catalog: "the second half of Drivers Ed"; "this quarter course"

courses.course_name: Essential Math for College and Career (EMC2)
courses.description: This course, designed in collaboration with Vermont State College System (VSCS), Vermont Agency of Education (AOE) and Vermont Student Assistance Corporation (VSAC), is a pilot course that is designed to ensure that seniors, who have studied math through Algebra II, are ready for college-level math after high school. This class will revisit essential concepts and skills from Numbers and Operations, Algebra, Functions, Geometry and Data and Statistics. Using hands-on problem-solving tasks, EMC2 will strengthen your foundational math skills, your critical-thinking skills, and give you a chance to show what you know through alternate assessment methods. This course emphasizes understanding of math concepts and not memorizing algorithms. You will engage in real-world applications and problem-solving tasks that require you to work with others and communicate your thinking process. Successful students will learn the math skills necessary to succeed in college and careers. The Vermont State College System (VSCS) has agreed that successful completion of this course will qualify students to enroll in credit bearing college math at any VSCS school without the need for remediation. Prerequisite: Algebra II
courses.offering_note: listed only in the 2024-25 West Rutland catalog, not in the newer Quarry Valley catalog
courses.notes: 2024-25 catalog supplement. Listed under BUSINESS and again under MATHEMATICS. Pilot course.

courses.description: Students in Analytical Writing About Film will view a variety of selected films dating from the 1940’s to the present. Students will learn to analyze film content and style, and to assess their effects on audiences and society at large for their impact on culture and society. The course will also explore connections between literature and film. Students will practice analytical and critical writing in this course, which will promote multiple literacies of cinematic narrative, characterization, setting and language. Students would need to be able to access films either through the internet, rental, or their local libraries. Film choices this semester include: Casablanca; Psycho; The Godfather; One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, The Breakfast Club, Shawshank Redemption, Slumdog Millionaire, American Sniper.
courses.offering_note: listed only in the 2024-25 West Rutland catalog, not in the newer Quarry Valley catalog

courses.description: This course is broken into three different educational areas. One component is college and career research. This work is designed to continue the work from student PLPs from previous years and help students make informed decisions about their future goals. The second component is working in an elementary classroom as a student aide. The third component is working on life skills, these include but not limited to, job applications, college applications, scholarship writing, personal finance, resume writing, and goal setting.

courses.description: The Media Literacy course focuses on current events and issues and on fundamental skills in critical thinking about media. Course goals include: ● Engaging with and reflecting on news articles on a weekly basis. ● Discussing current events and issues with a small group. ● Learning about current issues through documentary films and critiquing those films. ● Analyzing how controversial issues are covered in the news. ● Understanding the first amendment and censorship. ● Analyzing bias and media trust.

courses.description: Teachers and other staff members often request the assistance of upperclassmen as student aids for one period each day. These student aids are responsible for reporting to their assigned teacher or staff member and carrying out non-supervisory tasks as directed. Prospective aids will be interviewed by the teacher or staff prior to final assignment. Students will be assigned a study hall if attendance, behavior, or quality of work is not appropriate. The student will be evaluated quarterly. One full credit will be given for the completion of one full school year. No more than one credit may be earned as a student aid per year.

courses.description: Foundations level courses will be for students who need to develop the basic and functional life skills in the content area of the course. These are students who will benefit from small groups and a hands on approach to learning. This course is for students who need a functional/life-skills approach to the Social Studies Curriculum. Students enrolled in this course will apply geographic and civic responsibilities to real life situations. This course employs an interactive and hands-on approach that will enable the students to work at their own pace and learning style. They will develop an understanding of the importance of playing an active role in their community. Along with that, the students will also develop an understanding of social, economic, and political events as they affect their lives and their community. Recommendation by a team of teachers and instructor is required.

courses.course_name: CCV English Composition - Dual Enrollment Credit
courses.description: This is a college level course offered at WRS to juniors and seniors. In this course, students develop effective composition skills and research techniques. Students learn strategies for organizing, evaluating, and revising their work through extensive reading of a variety of essay styles and literary texts; apply writing and research techniques to their papers; and demonstrate proficiency in first-year college-level writing and information literacy.

courses.course_name: CCV Contemporary World Literature - Dual Enrollment Credit
courses.description: This college level course offered to juniors and seniors, introduces a variety of works of contemporary world literature. Through readings in fiction, drama and poetry,this course explores the range of human experience across national and cultural boundaries. Students will be 1. Define basic literary elements such as theme, character, plot, imagery, point of view, and narrative technique, and explain how these elements are used to express ideas, emotions, and values in specific works of literature. 2. Identify major themes in contemporary world literature. 3. Critically read, analyze, and evaluate examples of contemporary literature authored by representatives of a broad selection of nations and cultures. 4. Examine the social, political, and cultural circumstances that prompt the creation of various forms of literature. 5. Analyze the images of traditional cultures and individuals as presented in the works read.

courses.description: AP Calculus is an introductory calculus course using a modern approach to a classic subject. Graphing calculators allow the use of numerical and graphical methods that are more directly related to concepts, in addition to algebraic methods. This allows students with average algebra skills (and strong study skills) to be successful in calculus. AP Calculus is presented as the study of four fundamental concepts: limits, derivatives, definite and indefinite integrals. Students planning to pursue technical fields in college are highly recommended to enroll in this course. This course prepares students to take the respective AP exam. Many colleges will award college credit when students submit an official AP score report showing test scores of 3 or higher. Prerequisite: Students must have completed Pre-Calculus and have recommendation of prior year math teacher.

courses.description: The AP U.S. History course focuses on developing students’ understanding of American history from approximately 1491 to the present. The course has students investigate the content of U.S. history for significant events, individuals, developments, and processes in nine historical periods, and develop and use the same thinking skills and methods (analyzing primary and secondary sources, making historical comparisons, chronological reasoning, and argumentation) employed by historians when they study the past. The course also provides seven themes (American and national identity; migration and settlement; politics and power; work, exchange, and technology; America in the world; geography and environment; and culture and society) that students explore throughout the course in order to make connections among historical developments in different times and places. This course prepares students to take the respective AP exam. Many colleges will award college credit when students submit an official AP score report showing test scores of 3 or higher. Prerequisite: Students must have completed Global Studies II.

courses.description: West Rutland School partners with Educere to provide students with online courses. Students may only take an online course if 1) the course is not offered at WRS or 2) there is a course conflict within their schedule. If the course is offered at WRS and there is no conflict, students must take the course with a WRS teacher. Students who take online courses must be prepared to communicate regularly with their instructor via email and phone. Participation in online courses requires students to be self-disciplined and responsible enough to work independently. It is the student’s responsibility to log on, complete and submit all work, and communicate with the course instructor. Depending on whether or not the course of interest is a graduation requirement, there may be an up-front fee involved by the family. This will be reimbursed upon successful completion of the course. Please contact the Guidance Office for more information.

courses.description: With the Flexible Pathways bill (S.130/Act 77), dual enrollment vouchers allow Vermont high school students to take two college courses at any of 17 Vermont colleges or universities tuition-free. Students can use two vouchers throughout their junior and senior year but they must be used prior to graduation. Students will receive 1.0 credit per semester course upon the receipt of an official college transcript.

courses.description: CCV offers a free, non-credit Introduction to College Studies (ICS) course for high school students each semester. ICS prepares you for college by helping you set goals, problem-solve, manage time and stress, improve communication skills, take better notes, reduce test anxiety, and plan financially. This course is recommended to be taken during the summer between a student’s sophomore and junior year. This course is in addition to the two free dual enrollment vouchers.

courses.description: Vermont’s Early College Program allows high school seniors to take a full year of college-level classes while completing their high school degree. The Early College Program (ECP) simultaneously serves as a student's senior year of high school and first year of college. Students may take a year-long course of study in any discipline. This program is funded through the Flexible Pathways bill for approved colleges. Students who are accepted into an ECP must withdraw from West Rutland School prior to registering for enrollment at the college/university. Students will re-enroll at West Rutland School at the completion of their ECP in order to receive a West Rutland School diploma. Participating colleges/universities: Castleton University, Community College of Vermont, Goddard College, Northern Vermont University at Johnson or Lyndon, Norwich University and Vermont Technical College: Vermont Academy of Science and Technology.
